title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: Let the Games Begin
author: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning
summary: This is the Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning's weekly 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday digest, themed around a school rivalry week. It covers three research items with a classroom move for each: Gavin Kilduff's studies showing that rivals improve running times but also raise cheating and cutting corners; the open-access follow-up on John Wooden's coded teaching moves, showing his seemingly improvised practices were tightly planned on 3x5 cards; and a Cal Poly batting study in which randomly ordered pitch types beat blocked practice over the long term. A closing item recounts the Tokyo Olympics high jump in which two athletes chose to share gold. The curators' editorial framing and 'Try this' suggestions make the issue useful in its own right as a compact guide to competition, planning, and interleaving.
points: Rivalry boosts motivation and performance but also raises the odds of cutting corners, so rotate competing groups or let teams compete while members cooperate.
Wooden's apparent improvisation rested on detailed planning on 3x5 index cards and brief, warm, specific corrective feedback aimed at the act, not the actor.
Interleaved practice looked worse in the moment but produced far larger long-term gains than blocked practice in the Cal Poly batting study.
Smooth practice can create an illusion of performance that fools both student and teacher, so teachers should mix problem types on homework.
quotes: Their explanation is that a rival raises the stakes for how we see ourselves (and how we think others see us), and people cut more corners when that happens.
Wooden often looked like he was improvising, but in reality he and his assistants spent the bulk of their mornings planning practice down to minute details, all distilled on simple 3x5 index cards.
Wooden often praised the value of repetition, but in reality he was really orchestrating tightly scripted deliberate practice each day with feedback oriented at the act, and not the actor.
As we know from the great book Make It Stick, the blocked hitters looked better in the moment. They connected at a higher rate, while the random group struggled.
Over the long term, however, the random group improved by 56.7% whereas the blocked group saw only 24.8% gains.
But it’s a useful picture of what Kirschner, Hendrick, and Heal call the illusion of performance: a smooth practice session can fool the student and the teacher at the same time.
If you run review games or class competitions, rotate teams so that no teams or groups face one another consistently, or make the “opponent” the class’s score from last time.
Plan tomorrow’s class on a single index card and leave the back blank. While students work, jot down what specific students need in the moment.
